speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head O of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This year's Budget aside from the understandable focus on the evolving COVID-19 situation, has emphasised the importance of staying united and advancing forward as one people, to meet the challenges of the next decade and beyond.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a strategy that should be applied to healthcare planning as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And we have to come together as one people to think, to talk, to act and to prepare our country for the health challenges we face as we move towards 2030 and beyond.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The human body works well if all of its various component parts – the cells, the tissues and the organs – work together.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Disease and illness occur if one or more of these parts lose their close cooperation and their balance with other parts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The traditional model for the practice of medicine involves a close but often exclusive doctor-patient relationship, although not always with the same unity of purpose.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Health and healthcare policies in the past have also often proceeded on a typically prescriptive and directive approach, presumably because there is often a fair degree of information asymmetry, and also because admittedly, many of us could not always be relied on to make the right choices for our personal health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But health is not simply a numbers game and I was very supportive of more recent announcements by MOH that encouraged a mindset and strategic shifts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as whole-of-Government actions are needed to tackle complex issues confronting our country, a whole-of-society approach would be needed to cover that last hundred yards in our healthcare journey.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And in order to do this, we really need the unity of purpose amongst all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is certainly something that is not easy to achieve and certainly very difficult to budget for.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore's response to the COVID-19 situation is a timely illustration of the importance of societal unity to meet medical shocks.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many commentators have commented favourably on the quality of our disease preparedness planning, healthcare facilities, medical manpower, contact tracing, border controls and so on, and allow me to join my Parliamentary colleagues to put on record my sincere appreciation for the sacrifices that all frontline personnel, whether medical or otherwise, have made since the situation unfolded from the start of the year.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But one of the key elements to the success of the strategy is community involvement and how the whole of Singaporean society has come together to face this challenge.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is one critical element that Prof Dale Fisher, who was part of the WHO-China mission to Wuhan, noted as one key reason why China seems to be succeeding in controlling this outbreak and why Singapore is likewise having some success in managing the outbreak thus far.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And such community involvement would likewise be critical if we are to succeed in winning other wars we have, for example, the war on diabetes, on controlling dengue, bringing smoking rates down and getting everyone to eat better, sleep better and exercise more.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we work together to encourage each and every one of us to work together towards common health objectives?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of the major shifts that the Ministry had announced were to shift care from hospital to the community and to move from healthcare to health.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that this can be facilitated by rethinking some of our basic models of healthcare delivery and I hope that the planning of future healthcare facilities like polyclinics and hospitals will consider new models of care, with better integration and interaction between healthcare and community stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The hospital also provides novel community outreach programs, for example, we have a free, regular bus shuttle services from the nearby neighbourhoods which they serve to the hospital.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The hospital itself may be old and some parts are even heritage properties, but the way it functions is very much at the cutting edge of healthcare service provision.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I foresee that there will be increasing disruptions to the way healthcare is delivered and consumed.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hopefully, these disruptions would mostly be beneficial by improving efficiency and improving quality and accessibility and in this way, reducing costs as well as manpower requirements.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have previously asked about progress on integrating data analytics and perhaps even personalised medicine into our healthcare ecosystem and would like to ask if the Ministry has any updates on this front.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that fostering a united, whole-of-society approach to health, would require better health information accessibility and integration.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The excellent system of information dissemination during the COVID-19 crisis by battling disinformation and misinformation has certainly contributed much to controlling the outbreak and maintaining societal confidence in the measures the Government is taking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you are old, your eyesight is not so good, you have trouble moving, it may be more difficult for you to go to your nearby polyclinic or hospital.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our excellent performance by most measures, paradoxically means that it becomes harder and harder to make meaningful improvements in the future, as quality of our health is a more nuanced assessment than looking at crude rates like life expectancy or disease burden.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, I believe that a united society will be a key piece to this puzzle, and I look forward to the Ministry of Health's stewardship in this regard.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: May we all live long, live well and grow old together as one people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, the COVID-19 outbreak has put into focus the high quality of healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our healthcare workforce has truly shown courage and determination.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would there be further investment needed in the healthcare system, over and above the 2020 goals so as to have the extra capacity needed to deal with a future outbreak, if one was to occur?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MOH has achieved progress in many aspects of our public healthcare in the past decade.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During my nine years in Parliament so far, I have witnessed many measures introduced to enhance senior care capacity and capability, improve public healthcare affordability, increase healthcare manpower, enhance healthcare accessibility, war on diabetes and many other schemes to promote healthy living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And of course, in most recent times, a very successful campaign against COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And I hope that we can continue in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With so much done and taking stock, I would like to ask the Minister if we have achieved what we set out to achieve at the beginning of the Healthcare 2020 masterplan?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now that we are in 2020, what is the Ministry's vision for the next decade?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How hopeful can we be in moving from "curative" healthcare to "preventive" healthcare?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Our children and young people were increasingly overweight.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Following the declaration of War on Diabetes, the Prime Minister spoke of diabetes as one of the three key long-term issues for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give us a report of progress from the front?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What are our new and continuing efforts and plans; strategies and tactics?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: WHO had shared that it was "very impressed" with our measures.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Dr Zhang Wenhong (张文宏), Director of the Infectious Diseases Department at China's Fudan University, even drew parallels between our healthcare strategies with the famed Wudang (武当) martial art fighting techniques.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the COVID-19 situation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are our contingency preparations in readiness for possible scenarios ahead?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Specifically, what are our plans should community transmission within Singapore become more widespread or the evolving pandemic worsen, increasing the risk or reported infections once again.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Have we considered the scenarios in which the virus becomes endemic?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How then can we learn to leave with the virus?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Globally, many healthcare workers at the frontline have been infected while caring for patients and some have even lost their lives though fortunately, not to the same extent as was seen with SARS.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What actions are being taken to enhance protection for our frontline healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I know recent cases in Singapore where individuals have been charged for being evasive about the movements.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Is the Ministry considering expanded powers to access location and other related data from mobile devices of patients and close contacts for contact tracing?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: South Korea for instance has enacted laws after the MERS crisis in 2015 on managing the information of patients in an infectious disease outbreak.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the treatment front, a resident who was a SARS patient told me that a medical team visited her recently to obtain some blood samples to aid the COVID-19 cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some medical experts overseas have opined that using convalescent blood plasma from former SARS patients could assist very sick COVID-19 patients but was unlikely to be deployable on a larger scale.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could Ministry elaborate on the thinking and efforts on this front?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the virus is assessed to be spread by droplets at close range, containing the spread via separation measures like quarantine appears to be appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the preliminary assessments of the effectiveness of the Government's strategy so far?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore has a formidable healthcare force – the manner in which the COVID-19 outbreak is being dealt with reflects the dedication and professionalism of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is a precedent – a standard operating procedure of sorts – being presently developed by the Ministry such that the current operational experiences can be referenced by future healthcare workers in the event of a future outbreak of similar or different magnitude?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This will bolster our fight in any future outbreak.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: With our ageing population and the increasing burden of chronic diseases, will Government subsidies be able to keep pace with ever rising medical expenditures?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How will MOH ensure that our healthcare expenditure remains sustainable?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: MediSave, which is one of the central pillars of our healthcare financing system, is meant to provide for bigger medical expenses such as hospitalisation, day surgery and also outpatient expenses.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: However, very often, surgeries and hospital stays could be averted with early detection and intervention.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: If we could encourage more Singaporeans to work closely with their primary care providers, take preventive measures and actively monitor their medical conditions to arrest or slow their progress, we would be able to cut our healthcare expenditure significantly.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Hence, would the Ministry consider implementing measures to further reduce out-of-pocket expenses for primary care costs, including liberalising MediSave for more categories of outpatient expenses or fine-tuning, tweaking some of the existing Flexi-MediSave systems?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The principle of co-payment underpins our healthcare financing system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It was meant to encourage prudent and responsible use of healthcare resources to motivate Singaporeans to stay healthy.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: However, for the elderly, it is more challenging for them to keep illnesses at bay.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Many of them worry that even with Government subsidies, they might have difficulty affording the co-payment component of some of the medical expenses.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How does MOH plan to keep healthcare affordable for Singaporeans, particularly for senior citizens?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Out-of-pocket expenses for medical care when our seniors enter their 60s can be a source of significant insecurity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We also know from previous Parliamentary replies over the years that elderly patients above 60 years of age with chronic conditions visited polyclinics and CHAS clinics an average of six times a year, with an average annual bill of $200 after subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those without chronic illnesses visited these healthcare facilities on average about three times a year, with an average annual bill of about $60 after subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe there is scope to increase the Flexi-MediSave limits, particularly those who have larger outpatient bills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party acknowledges that higher withdrawal limits based on MediSave balances must be carefully considered as it may result in some Singaporeans having less MediSave savings through retirement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, each senior Singaporean's situation is different, particularly in view of differing MediSave balances across seniors in the population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, Sir, a differentiated ceiling for seniors has been replicated for other MediSave schemes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, from this year, a differentiated MediSave withdrawal scheme has been introduced for Singaporeans with long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Individuals with $20,000 or more in their MediSave account will be allowed to use $200 each month or $2,400 per year from MediSave for long-term care.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans with balances of between $15,000 and above are allowed to $150 per month, and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from increasing the Flexi-MediSave limits for outpatient treatment, the additional flexibility in the form of a differentiated ceiling should also be considered to allow for inpatient co-payments that have to be paid in cash after MediSave deductions, particularly as our seniors grow older.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While MediShield Life and existing MediSave withdrawals can be utilised for inpatient bills, many patients are still required to make out-of-pocket payments in cash because of existing MediSave limits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just this Monday at my Meet-the-People Session (MPS), I saw a resident who asked me to write to the authorities to allow his 75-year-old brother – unemployed and living alone – to utilise around $1,400 from his MediSave to settle his hospitalisation bills.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He showed me his brother's CPF statement and the amount stood in excess of $51,000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, there is further scope to further assist our seniors and reduce their out-of-pocket expenses for healthcare-related expenditure.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not a call for additional subsidies that impact the healthcare budget but a better calibrated MediSave regime that allows our seniors to better manage their cost of living concerns and give them a greater peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is made available at polyclinics islandwide as well as the restructured hospitals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have encountered residents who defaulted their medical appointments especially those who have multiple appointments in a month, as they are too weak to travel by bus or train, and they do not have the financial means to take a taxi or private hire car to ferry them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I do know of Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs) that offer subsidies for private ambulance fee to needy individuals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, this subsidised fee is still too high and unaffordable for some.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Allowing MediFund Scheme to be used for reimbursement of transport fare will surely ease the financial struggles and, more importantly, will enhance the accessibility of medical treatments for this group.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, you can take both cuts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In my cut earlier, I mentioned that public healthcare affordability has improved over the years that I have seen in this House.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But in the course of my constituency work, I still meet many middle-age and senior residents who continue to worry about healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: One of the issues they face is not being able to use more of their MediSave to pay for their medical bills, forcing them to make out-of-pocket payments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: A common argument I have heard from affected residents is that they still have savings in their MediSave, so why can they not use more of their own money for their own treatments?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Attempts to explain how CPF works cannot be the same as how a private bank account works were futile as they have immediate needs to solve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I have a resident, Mr Tay, who has a strong sense of self-pride and self-reliance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: While his wife and children are financially independent and he has a good relationship with them, he is highly reluctant to ask them to support his medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: He argues for more use of his MediSave beyond the current annual cap so that he can pay for his own needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Can we also conscientiously target our publicity and social outreach to encourage children with means to take the initiative to top up parents’ Medisave and Ordinary savings so that their parents need not feel the burden of having to ask their children for money?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There is no guarantee that the children will comply but it is a social signal that we should actively send.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Also, the community can play a role in raising resources to support seniors who need help with their medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Would MOH consider a matching fund to boost the funds raised for this purpose?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I once met a relatively young resident during my block visit, about my age or younger.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: He suffers from severe eczema, highly uncomfortable, and has difficulties finding or holding down jobs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: His parents are working but they are just typical 3-roomers and they worry about how they could continue to finance his skin treatments as they age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is a struggle for them and certainly tormenting for the young man himself.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: I serve in the MacPherson SMC, a 52-year-old community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: With a rapidly ageing population across Singapore, what are MOH’s plans beyond 2020 to keep care accessible for all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu, you can take both cuts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: By 2050, almost half of our population will be in this age group.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: As the elderly are four times more likely than younger Singaporeans to be hospitalised, there will be much greater demand for hospital beds.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry share an update on how it will ensure that we have enough capacity in our hospitals, the corresponding number of healthcare professionals and other necessary medical resources?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I would also like to ask the Minister if he has the capacity projections for our various healthcare institutions in the next 10, 20 and 30 years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These include general hospitals, community hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, day care and eldercare centres and, very importantly, day rehabilitation and dementia day care centres.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are MOH's plans to keep this care accessible?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Another one of my concerns is how we can better regulate and balance the capacity growth in public versus private healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Is there room for closer collaboration and greater permeability between our public and private sectors to optimise healthcare resources, particularly in times of emergency and crisis?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Presently, the Ministry already has such a partnership with Raffles Hospital for patients with non-critical medical conditions sent there by the Singapore Civil Defence Force emergency ambulances.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These patients will benefit from subsidised care at rates similar to those at our public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What is the progress on the areas of cooperation with the private sector to expand our national capacity?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: It has been demonstrated that health systems with a strong primary care sector produce better health outcomes by improving access to comprehensive care services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: They also keep medical expenditures lower in the long run.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Our primary care professionals are indeed the bedrock of our healthcare system here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Are the other seven clinics on track to be ready by 2030?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Minister share details of the types of services each polyclinic will offer?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Besides expanding our public sector primary care capacity, we should continue to strengthen our private sector as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Our vast network of private General Practitioner (GP) clinics has the benefit of delivering the personal "one patient, one doctor" service.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How will MOH support GPs in providing better holistic care?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How close are we to the ideal of "one patient, one doctor" in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Under the Primary Care Networks (PCN) scheme, GP clinics can organise themselves into networks to provide team-based care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on the progress of the PCN scheme?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Are there any new models for primary care delivery that the Ministry is considering?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPCs) system has also proven its value during this recent COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Are there plans to expand and strengthen this very useful initiative?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Three will be located in Serangoon, Kaki Bukit and Tengah and are slated to be ready by 2025.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The other seven will be located in Bukit Panjang, Eunos, Kallang, Sembawang, Khatib, Tampines North and Yew Tee.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is MOH on track to reach the target of opening these seven clinics by 2030?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the locations of these 10 polyclinics confirmed, there remains two more possible sites.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I strongly urge the Ministry to build one of these in Bishan.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the last few years, a few condominiums were built in Bishan.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the next few years, HDB will be adding many blocks too.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The profile of Bishan will be changed significantly with many more households and an increasing population of older residents.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As of today, the proportion of senior citizens in Bishan is already higher than the national average.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Presently, due to the lack of a polyclinic in Bishan, my residents have to travel to the polyclinics in Toa Payoh and Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As part of the journey, some of the elderly need to cross a pedestrian overhead bridge not served by elevators.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A polyclinic is a facility many residents are looking forward to.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also a necessity, so that the new households moving into Bishan will not overwhelm the polyclinics in Toa Payoh and Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides expanding public sector capacity, what are MOH's measures to support private GPs in providing better and holistic primary care for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: According to the Singapore Mental Health Study conducted in 2010, 5.8% of our adult population in Singapore suffered from Major Depressive Disorder some time in life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a stigma attached to mental conditions that stops people acknowledging them and seeking medical help.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is important to note these afflicted persons need medical care and treatment that can relieve them from their predicaments and bring them back to normality and happiness.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: As good community mental health provision will enable us to have better outreach to those afflicted, may I ask how MOH is ensuring this adequacy?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Raising awareness and educating more people about depression, especially on the symptoms of depression, such as suicidal thought, sleep disorder, feeling of hopelessness and loss of interest in daily activities, will prompt family members or friends to intervene earlier.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Seniors especially those living alone or those with no family support are more prone to having depression.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Last year, IMH said that stress-related anxiety and depressive disorders are common conditions seen at its Child Guidance Clinics which treat children aged six to 18.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our youths have long precious journeys in their lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: A majority of those with mental disorders do live at home.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Even those with major disorders are usually not hospitalised.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It is always a drain on the care-givers to look after those afflicted family members, especially those with major disorders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's efforts to ramp up mental wellness promotion are starting to bear fruit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, the increased prevalence rates in the 2016 study could be attributed to greater awareness and willingness to seek treatment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this also means that we are really only catching up to the true extent of mental health disorder and there are a lot more Singaporeans who remain undiagnosed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to focus instead on three other As – availability, accessibility and affordability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On availability, MOH announced in Budget 2017 that one in two polyclinics will have a mental wellness clinic, or a dementia clinic, or both, by 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There were already such clinics in seven of the 18 polyclinics in 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the Government should aim higher now and make mental wellness clinics available to Singaporeans in all 18 polyclinics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other issue is the availability of psychiatrists and psychologists, especially in the public health sector, as the 2016 study noted the low rate per 100,000 residents here compared to higher income countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there plans to improve on this front?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On accessibility, five of the seven wellness clinics in the polyclinics only see referred patients and the two Community Wellness Clinics run by IMH allow for consultation by appointments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Persons suffering from mental disorders are already finding it hard to come forward for treatment due to social stigma, thus we need to make the clinics as accessible as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Ministry make all mental wellness clinics at polyclinic open to consultation by appointment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe there is a need for the limit to be raised to at least $1,000 a year to make mental health treatments more affordable.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Ms Anthea Ong, you can take your four cuts together.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, how do we ensure that the quality of mental healthcare is on par with what Singapore is known for in healthcare?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Implementing a measurement feedback system (MFS), adopted in countries such as England, could is one way.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In the public consultation on mental health that my team and I conducted, 26 responses indicated feedback on treatment could improve their health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry clarify what measures are in place to ensure that there is regular feedback given by clients to their mental healthcare professionals?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is recommended by WHO and National Health Service (NHS) England that treatment for mental health conditions should be supported by talking therapies including counselling.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: From the consultation, 29 respondents described the importance of psychological support alongside medication in treating mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One elaborated that her husband did not fare well on medication alone, as "no trust was established (and) he did not open up".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider measures to ensure that individuals requiring mental healthcare be supported not only by psychiatrists and medications, but paired with psychotherapy and counselling?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: WHO encourages engaging stakeholders in the evaluation of mental health initiatives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar vein, could the Ministry share what measures have been undertaken to involve stakeholders, including people with lived experiences of mental health conditions, in evaluating initiatives launched under the Community Mental Health Masterplan?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In expanding mental healthcare into community settings, personnel including social workers and community counsellors now interact with issues of mental health, and steps should be taken to ensure they are appropriately qualified and competent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In continuity with a whole-of-Government approach, would the Ministry consider instituting a code of practice for non-medical personnel involved in mental healthcare, including psychologists, therapists and those within community settings such as social workers and community counsellors?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Next cut, which was initially directed to MSF.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: WHO suggests that the LGBTQ+ community should be considered as a vulnerable group in mental healthcare, with the double stigma of homophobia and seeking help for mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent public consultation on mental health that we conducted, 13 responses referenced such a double stigma.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: One lamented that "it doesn't help too with social stigma against mental health and LGBTQ+ that push more away from the care they need, like me." For the LGBTQ+ community, specific issues include discrimination by mental healthcare professionals as well as disclosing one's sexual and gender identities to family without consent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the Government's commitment to mental healthcare in community settings, we now have social workers and counsellors who support mental health, in addition to mental healthcare professionals such as psychiatrists and psychologists.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider adopting a whole-of-Government approach in ensuring that personnel working in mental healthcare, including those within community settings, are trained and competent in LGBTQ-related issues?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Diversity officers supporting minorities is a common practice in the business sector.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider appointing diversity officers, sited within respective agencies, across the healthcare and social services sectors?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They can serve as a resource for professionals to tap on to better understand LGBTQ-related issues, help to develop competencies in serving LGBTQ individuals and ensure dissemination of LGBTQ-specific resources.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We have come a long way in recognising mental health as an integral part of our total health, but still a long way to go in giving this priority and parity to physical health in our policies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Barriers to mental healthcare are significant issues facing many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure the Ministry wants to assure Singaporeans that there is no discrimination against those with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the high co-morbidity between those suffering from chronic physical health conditions and those with mental health conditions, how does the Ministry ensure this group of patients benefit from sufficient Medisave withdrawal limits for outpatient treatments?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In line with the spirit of the Community Mental Health Masterplan to shift mental healthcare from medical institutions into the community, would the Ministry consider allowing patients to tap on their MediSave for mental healthcare provided by community mental health services such Shan You Counselling Centre, Clarity, and Counselling and Care Centre?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry clarify on what plans are in store to improve these numbers so as to increase accessibility?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Seventy-one respondents shared that lack of clear, trusted and consolidated information on how to seek help limited their help-seeking behaviour.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are more than 10 helplines available under NCSS' Mental Health Resource Directory.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider setting up a centralised helpline – maybe 991 or something – to make it easier for a person in distress to call for help?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These helplines could even be manned by peer supporters, given the many community efforts to promote peer support training.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry also consider a centralised platform for mental health services to include information about service providers and treatment options available, estimated costs of treatment and available subsidies for treatment?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Building on the Ministry's community outreach efforts, would the Ministry consider expanding the modes of referral for community mental healthcare, including text or web-chats, phone calls, walk-ins, referral by friends and family, and also self-referral?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As subsidised referrals for public healthcare can only be made through public healthcare institutions, would the Ministry consider allowing professionals in community mental healthcare to make these subsidised referrals?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Although we have robust laws governing confidentiality in the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), there continues to be worries about access to one's mental health history within the public healthcare system, especially by employers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A respondent from the consultation shared that within the Public Service, a colleague's mental health condition was accessed through the public healthcare system and was shared as office gossip by supervisors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, respondents have shared with me their worries on the sharing of their personal information by mental healthcare professionals, including one who was threatened by her school counsellor that her parents will be informed of her same-sex relationship.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There are also instances of unnecessary declarations of mental health information, with a respondent indicating that she was unable to donate blood due to her mental health history.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, for persons with disabilities (PWDs), medical rehabilitation is always available.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: What is neither routinely recommended nor provided is any kind of mental health rehabilitation and support.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Discrimination and abuse add their own weight to the already present guilt and shame many PWDs experience.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: It prevents the PWD from speaking out against it or seeking external help to cope with it.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Can there be more information on where PWDs can seek access to mental healthcare if necessary?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: The idea persists that PWDs are disabled, not mentally challenged, and therefore do not require mental health support.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: This view serves only to perpetuate the stigma around mental health concerns and makes it extremely challenging for PWDs to access mental healthcare.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, in addition to providing better support for mental health issues at our workplaces, we also need to do our part to provide better mental health services at the community level, particularly for our youths and young adults.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If left unaddressed, this could significantly affect the mental well-being of the next generation of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am therefore glad that the Government has announced that it will create the Youth Mental Well-being Network, which will bring young Singaporeans together and look at ways to promote mental wellness for their generation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement will also do our part to foster better mental wellness among youths through our Young NTUC arm.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Young NTUC has since begun engaging with youths and young working adults to better understand the mental wellness issues that affect them as they transition from school to working life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Young NTUC is working to put together peer-to-peer support systems for our youths and I hope that the Government can partner with the Labour Movement to make mental wellness services more readily accessible to our young adults and youths.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to illustrate some of these challenges through three cases I dealt with in the recent past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first challenge is difficulty in detecting these cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I met a lady who sought some assistance to repair a water pipe in her kitchen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I arranged for a community volunteer to visit her.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No one, even her immediate neighbour, knew of hoarding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, the lady was staying with her daughter who was later identified as suffering from depression.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She used to receive from IMH but defaulted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Quite clearly, the lady and her daughter are unable to seek help on their own.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If not for the chance meeting between the mother and I, this case would not have been detected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second challenge we see on the ground is lack of cooperation on the part of care-givers, mostly because of lack of trust.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A few months back, I received a complaint from a resident of noise disturbance from his neighbour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I asked my community volunteer to help mediate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The family residing at the unit in question consists of three persons: father, mother and their young son.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My volunteer could immediately tell that the son was mentally unwell.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was not able to look at my volunteer in the eye.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was muttering to himself and pacing to and fro.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The parents related that he has a habit of shouting and banging on the walls, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My volunteer tried to convince the boy’s parents to admit him to IMH.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The father was, unfortunately, dead set against sending his son to IMH because of some unrelated incident that happened in the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the meantime, the poor neighbours continue to put up with the disturbance which happens in the wee hours of the night.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The third challenge is ignorance on the part of care-givers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recently met a couple at their home.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Their daughter, now in her 20s, has been holed up in her bedroom for years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She simply refused to come out from her room since she was in Secondary 3.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When I asked them why they decided not to ask for help earlier, they told me that they were worried that her daughter may end her life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They were plainly anguished by their daughter's condition but simply did not know what to do for years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, we should keep an eye and follow up on patients who are suffering from serious mental illnesses who have defaulted in their treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because treatment for such cases is focused on containing the situation, not to cure the patients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, if they are not receiving treatment, one can reasonably expect these patients to be in trouble.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This is not only includes traditional medicine practices, such as Traditional Chinese Medicine, Jammu and Ayurvedic medicine, but also includes practices such as Chiropractic and Homoeopathy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, not all types of CAMs are treated the same under our existing laws and regulations.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, regulations do not cover the Jammu or Ayurvedic practitioners or the product they sell.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Chiropractic practices popular amongst office worker has also seen an increasing number of complaints against practitioners in the field as reported by The Straits Times in 2016.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This has led to a call by the Chiropractic Association for Government regulation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The lack of regulation, particularly concerning the unregulated use of CAM practices, may lead to detrimental outcomes of patients who simultaneously see western-trained doctors alongside CAM practitioners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The Act can help to set regulations that imposes a minimum standard of protection against consumers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Such a regime should consider requiring mandatory registration for all CAM practitioners and mandatory information given to the patient about the underlying risks of using CAM.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This also should include the mandatory disclosure of usage of CAM treatment to healthcare medical practitioners when patients seek medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Such a regime should ensure regulation is in place for both CAM practitioners and patient that otherwise need to seek recourse elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, several Members of Parliament have asked about COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Dr Chia asked about contact tracing, we are indeed strengthening our capability on contact tracing efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to thank Singaporeans for their cooperation and support for the various measures we have implemented, without which, our efforts will not be effective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Globally, the number of cases outside mainland China continues to grow at an alarming rate across continents and regions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is worrying as they pose a high risk of importation of cases into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, we must expect to see significantly higher numbers of new cases in time to come.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In line with our risk assessment of the situation, we have implemented precautionary measures, including travel advisories and restrictions, temperature screening, contact tracing, quarantine, among others.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the effectiveness of our current strategy and how we can better prepare for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have to appreciate that every outbreak is different.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: COVID-19 is different from SARS and different from H1N1.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even as we do our best to learn from each outbreak and prepare for the next, we must always expect the unexpected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To mount a swift and effective response, we have to adopt a whole-of-Government approach and mobilise the resources of all the relevant agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will allow us to assess, decide and execute our response quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is important to be transparent, too and share the information we know as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will help to preserve the trust between the people and the Government so that we can have the support of the public as we work together to fight COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is also crucial to counter and respond decisively to fake news to avoid diversion of our resources and prevent disruption to our efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The international scientific community has been working hard to study the virus, share new findings and develop solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are sharing our best practices, research and knowledge on COVID-19 with other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, scientists from China published the genetic sequence of the COVID-19 virus quite early on, on 12 January 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our scientists are also participating in international clinical trials for treatment and vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about using blood plasma for treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are indeed planning to do so and NCID is collecting blood plasma from patients but there are limitations and constraints.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It may take some time before effective treatments and vaccines become available.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the global situation evolves, many countries may become infected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will become increasingly difficult to stop the virus at our borders as we cannot ban visitors from every country and shut ourselves out from the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even amongst our closest neighbours, the situation is also evolving.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, it is likely that we will continue to see more cases and this disease will stay with us for quite a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will have to continuously adjust, fine-tune our measures to deal with the disease so that life can go on while appropriate precautions are put in place.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am glad to see the SG Clean campaign picking up momentum and I would like to thank Minister Masagos for leading this important effort.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All of us have a role to play and we must continue the good practices that have proven effective in reducing the spread of infectious diseases – such as staying home when unwell, practising good personal hygiene.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am beginning to sound like a broken record, but sometimes broken records are good.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We should also maintain high public hygiene standards in our food centres and public toilets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will strengthen our collective resilience against COVID-19 as well as other infectious diseases, while allowing us to go about our daily lives as normally as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our healthcare workers are critical in our efforts in managing and containing this outbreak.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I want to assure Dr Chia Shi-Lu that they are well-trained on infection control and prevention, and are provided with the appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) for their safety.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The senior management of our three healthcare clusters have informed me that as a gesture of solidarity with our healthcare workers, they will donate their own Special Bonuses to the staff welfare fund of their respective clusters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The details of the Special Bonus for our healthcare workers will be released in due course, but for now our focus is to keep up our fight to contain the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, even as we tackle the COVID-19 outbreak, we need to continue to plan forward and build our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: MOH first introduced Healthcare 2020 in 2012 to increase accessibility, raise quality and enhance the affordability of healthcare services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are now in 2020, Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Tin Pei Ling have all asked how we have fared with regard to Healthcare 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, I must say I did not expect to still be Minister for Health in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But I am still Minister for Health and I am happy to share that MOH has delivered on what we promised.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have invested significantly in infrastructure to add capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In 2019 alone, we opened the National University Centre for Oral Health Singapore and Outram Community Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Sengkang General and Community Hospitals, which first began seeing patients in 2018, were also officially opened in 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Of course, we also opened the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID) in time for this COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We stepped up building of long-term care facilities too like nursing homes and daycare centres to meet the needs of our ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We continued to improve the quality of care, with significant expansion in medical school and nursing intakes to ensure sufficient healthcare manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We expanded our polyclinic and GP networks, and further integrated patient care through the introduction of team-based care, and strengthened referral pathways to our Specialists Outpatient Clinics (SOCs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have made healthcare more affordable for all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over the years, we have progressively enhanced and expanded the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) to make primary care more affordable and for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also introduced the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages in 2014 and 2019 to help our senior generations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Tong will go into greater details later on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Most importantly, our overall healthcare outcomes have improved, with longer life expectancy and Health Adjusted Life Expectancy (HALE).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This means that Singaporeans are not only living longer but living longer in good health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singaporeans are still living about 10 years in ill health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To combat chronic diseases, we declared War on Diabetes in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To overcome this fearsome adversary, we have to start at the ground level, to build a strong foundation by shaping an eco-system that encourages healthier choices like living healthy lives and staying physically active.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While healthier lives for Singaporeans will take many years of effort to realise, some of our efforts have yielded early progress.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, we have created more options for healthier meals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As of 2019, one in two stalls across hawker centres and coffeeshops listed at least one healthier option on their menu, as part of the Healthier Dining Programme (HDP).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The prevalence of regular leisure-time exercise has also increased by about six percentage points from 29% to 35% between 2017 and 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be launching a public campaign later this year to increase awareness on regular diabetic foot and eye screening.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With greater awareness, we hope to reduce the incidence of lower limb amputation and give our patients better quality of life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These are just some of the many efforts we are taking on preventive healthcare that Ms Tin Pei Ling has asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin will be sharing more on our efforts later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Besides prevention, we are also providing greater support for individuals living with diabetes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Under our Patient Empowerment for Self-care Framework, we have developed the National Diabetes Reference Materials on HealthHub, as a comprehensive resource for patients and their care-givers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is helpful for patients and families as they can "self-help" themselves to information about their condition and what they can do for better disease management.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, patients who wish to start exercising can learn simple, safe and practical ways to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These materials can also be customised by healthcare professionals for their own patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our healthcare clusters will also be commencing pilot programmes from the second half of 2020 to increase patients' ownership of their care journeys.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, one of the programmes will empower newly diagnosed patients with diabetes to initiate and sustain lifestyle changes through group health coaching and greater peer support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To win the war on diabetes we will need concerted, multi-year efforts and many of these efforts will only bear fruit in the long-term.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, we will continue to monitor the intermediate outcomes, like physical activity and dietary practices to better track the progress of our various initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Going forward, I would like to assure Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Christopher de Souza that we will continue to invest in new healthcare infrastructure and facilities to ensure care continues to be accessible to meet the needs of the ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be opening four more new polyclinics in over the next two years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Lam will share more about the expansion plans for our polyclinics later on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Woodlands Health Campus is scheduled to open progressively from 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We had experienced some challenges during the construction due to soil conditions, but we have mostly caught up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Now, with COVID-19, we are discussing with our contractors and suppliers to assess the impact and we hope to minimise delays.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Other upcoming facilities include a new community hospital in Novena and the redevelopment of two national specialist centres, that is, the new National Cancer Centre and the National Skin Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: MOH had previously announced that National University Health Systems (NUHS) would design new and innovative care models and test them at the Alexandra Hospital (AH) as part of AH's future development.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The master planning exercise of AH was completed in 2019 and we will be calling tender soon for Medical Planners for this project.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling has asked about healthcare capacity in the east.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Changi General Hospital (CGH) is currently the only hospital in the east.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While we have added significant capacity in CGH through expansion over the years, the healthcare demand has grown substantially as a result of population growth and ageing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While the hospital will include the normal range of hospital services, we also want to hear what the community would like to see in this new hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As such, SingHealth, which will be operating this new hospital, will be engaging the community to co-create ideas to better meet the needs of the residents there.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: SingHealth will reach out to the community leaders when they are ready to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Expanding our healthcare system will also mean that expenditure on healthcare will grow, both in the development cost of building new facilities, and later on, as the cost of operating these facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Of this 11%, about five percentage points of this 11% increase was due to increased utilisation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As our population ages and grows, demand for healthcare services also increases, as some Members of Parliament observed earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are also utilising more healthcare than in the past, even after accounting for ageing and population growth.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is partly the result of making care more accessible and affordable to all, and partly due to earlier diagnosis, closer monitoring and follow-ups for medical conditions, that means, more frequent consultations and treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The range of treatment options has also expanded as the frontiers of medicine advance, increasing utilisation, but at the same time, improving lifespans and the quality of life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is five percentage points of the 11%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Approximately, another four percentage points of the growth in national health expenditure can be attributed to higher manpower costs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the one hand, our healthcare workforce expanded significantly between 2012 and 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, our healthcare workers' salaries also increased as we implemented pay adjustments to attract and retain our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, that is four and five, that, is nine percentage points out of 11%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The remaining two percentage points have largely been due to increases in the costs of drugs, medical devices and other overheads.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And as Deputy Prime Minister highlighted in his Budget 2020 round-up speech, we can expect that the overall national health expenditure will continue to increase as our population ages and we step up our investments in facilities and services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But we must continue to be prudent in our healthcare expenditure to ensure that it is directed towards where it gives us the best outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, to answer Dr Chia and Ms Tin Pei Ling's questions on what our strategy is going forward, we must continue on our transformation journey for healthcare to ensure we have a good and sustainable system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We must press on with our efforts to go beyond healthcare to health, beyond hospital to community and beyond quality to value.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We can make wise decisions and choices and have a trusted family physician to turn to for advice.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Only then can we ensure that our healthcare system is sustainable and remains affordable for our patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Information technology (IT) will continue to be an essential enabler for our healthcare system, and we will continue to strengthen our governance and safeguards on our data.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will be essential to maintain the public's trust.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over the past year, we have been taking concrete steps to implement the recommendations of the Committee of Inquiry (COI) on the SingHealth cyber attack.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These steps will help to raise the cybersecurity posture of the public healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The more complex measures require careful implementation to avoid disrupting essential healthcare services and impacting patient safety.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Various enhancements have also been made to strengthen the security of the National Electronic Health Records (NEHR).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Work is still on-going and the enhancements are being implemented.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mandatory contribution to NEHR will be deferred until all enhancements are completed and we are satisfied that the system is assessed to be sufficiently robust.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will further updates at the appropriate juncture.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: While we secure our systems, we continue to explore new technologies, such as telemedicine, how they can improve care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To-date, 25 public healthcare institutions and 39 community care partners have started video consultation pilot services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will also leverage technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence, machine learning and robotics to support the work in public healthcare, which Dr Chia has asked about in his cut.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: SELENA+ has proven to be more efficient in delivering fast and accurate results.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To conclude, shaping better healthcare in Singapore is not something that MOH and our healthcare providers can do alone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Everyone will have a role to play in this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We can start by taking care of our own health – by taking responsibility to keep ourselves healthy, we can live better, longer and healthier lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, if I may, let me speak in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (In Mandarin):   To battle COVID-19, we must be calm and not panic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As long as we take the right precautions, pay attention to personal hygiene, we can carry on with our day-to-day activities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Last Sunday, together with Minister Masagos and a few colleagues, I went to the Teck Whye Garden in Choa Chu Kang to take part in their community morning exercise that was just resumed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am heartened to see that so many of our residents are committed to staying healthy and actively participate in activities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: (In English): Sir, keeping everyone healthy is a team effort and we are all part of that team.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, let us all play our part to keep Singapore and Singaporeans in good health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Chairman, our healthcare workers have been working tirelessly since the onset of the COVID-19 outbreak to combat the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Many have suspended vacations and put in extra hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I commend all healthcare workers – nurses, doctors, medics, and more – for putting your lives on the line to serve Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Indeed, healthcare workers are a special group of professionals and I urge our tripartite partners to come together to do more for them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: One, let us recognise them not only when we have a crisis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Two, let us ramp up recruitment efforts and bring in more local talents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: And three, let us reduce attrition and address the reasons why some leave service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: While I commend the Ministry's "Care To Go Beyond" campaign, which profiles the work of nurses to attract locals into the industry, more needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Perhaps the Ministry can consider recruiting more mid-career nurses in their 50s and place them in wards that are less intense.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: At 59 years old, Mdm Wan finally achieved her childhood ambition of becoming a nurse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: More details of her story and other inspiring stories of those who have found nursing to be their calling in life can be found on my blog post today – because I only have limited time here!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Some do not return because they feel that their skills are out of touch.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The union is also discussing how to provide training to these nurses through its Healthcare Academy – training that are relevant and timely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: I hope that the Ministry can work with the Labour Movement to improve retention of nurses and to encourage those who have left service to return to nursing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Chairman, Sir, even as we honour our frontline healthcare workers in this COVID-19 situation, we should make sure that we protect them in three ways: physical health and safety, mental wellness and social well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On physical health and safety, the most heartbreaking COVID-19 news are those on doctors and nurses getting infected and succumbing to the disease.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: A recent article by Dr Gan Wee Hoe and Dr Chia Kee Seng published in The Straits Times gave details on some measures taken to protect the health and safety of our healthcare workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Would the Minister share the key measures implemented to protect our healthcare workers' own health and safety?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On mental wellness, again, based on the SARS experience, frontline healthcare workers suffer from high levels of burn-out and post-traumatic stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Would the Minister please share whether any mental health resources are made available to our healthcare workers in this crisis, and whether free counselling and mental health resources can be made available to our frontline healthcare workers for the years after this crisis has blown over?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On social well-being, reports of healthcare workers in uniform being ostracised in public bring back ugly memories from the SARS epidemic, where about half of local healthcare workers experienced some form of social stigmatisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I think it is amazing to see how many Singaporeans are fighting back to show appreciation to our frontline workers in concrete ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Nevertheless, I want to raise two points here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: First, are healthcare workers afforded any legal protection from being abused when they are in uniform, whether at work or in public?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Second, in a recent Straits Times report on the ostracisation of nurses in uniform, healthcare leaders reassured the public that the uniforms do not pose any risk of infection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: After this crisis has blown over, it may be timely to rethink whether uniforms are important for nurses or they should, like doctors, go to work in office attire and change to professional scrubs at work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am ambivalent about this as I grew up watching my mum go to work in her nurse uniform and I am still immensely proud of her.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: She related to me some of the obstracisation she experienced during SARS and how it forced her to change out of uniform to return home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Thus, I would rather see a change in public attitude.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These personalised, coordinated and fully-subsidised care services play a crucial role in preventive care for the less privileged seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the nurses visit their patients in their homes, they are better able to detect the environment, social and other factors affecting their health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This enables them to have a more holistic understanding of their patients' needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over time, patients build trust in their nurses and this makes it easier for them to open up and accept their nurses' advice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The posts are currently located at Senior Activity Centres.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will MOH partner with other organisations such as other Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs) to expand the location options for future posts, as this will bring care closer to home for seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How many nurses are working under this scheme and how many more will MOH recruit to cope with the increasing number of elderly persons in the coming years?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the ratio of community nurses to residents under their charge?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How has the retention rate of the nurses been so far?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
