text: Allied healthcare workers such as physiotherapists, speech therapists, nurses, medical support staff all play a significant role in the overall care for the patient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Methods to increase opportunities and training for their career and wage advancements are also key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This will ensure that a strong, core body of well-trained allied healthcare workers can pass down their experiences and knowledge to successive cohorts.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Irene Quay, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore and the Assistant Director of Allied Health Office at KK Women's and Children's Hospital.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke during the Employment (Amendment) Bill debate in 2018 on allowing AHPs and CPPs to issue recognised medical certificates (MCs).

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently under the Medical Registration Act, only qualified medical practitioners are able to issue medical certificates.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As our ageing population increases along with the surge in chronic diseases, we need to change our approach towards long-term follow-up for chronic patients to ensure healthcare and financial sustainability.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: AHPs and CPPs need to have the right tools to step up in their roles to care for these patients.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, it is reassuring to see more of them taking over follow-up appointments for chronic cases as well as being equipped to manage them.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, they are handicapped for reasons pertaining to regulatory restrictions.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Patients often require MCs after consultation and they will have to be directed to medical doctors for issuances of MCs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This can be piloted through a regulatory sandbox approach.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, Public services can also take the lead to recognise time sheets and reimbursement for minor ailments and medication from retail pharmacies to relieve our polyclinics from their heavy workload.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar vein, I understand that MOH has been attempting to right-site chronic disease patients to be cared for in the community by AHPs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the success of this shift so far and the projected targets for the next five years?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that the current financial gradient may not be steep enough to facilitate this shift from acute to the community.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: If done right, I see potential to effect an even more efficient and financially sustainable healthcare system for our citizens.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in this COS speech, I would like to address the need to direct support towards pharmacists in tackling medication-related issues within the community.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: One such issue is polypharmacy, which is the concurrent use of multiple medication.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is a growing and persistent issue in Singapore as our population rapidly ages alongside with an increase in the number of patients with chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: In the previous committee hearing, I talked about the different types of medication waste.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For this year's committee hearing, I would like to highlight another grave medication-related problem in our healthcare system – medication non-adherence or compliance.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This issue is especially prevalent among the elderly.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This makes up about 35% of newly diagnosed diabetes patients in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: There are many reasons for medication non-adherence, which include a lack of understanding or knowledge of diabetic medicine, difficulty in managing their complex medication regimen, concerns about medication side-effects and cultural beliefs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Another study by the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health and the Department of Pharmacy in NUS shows that pharmacists play an important role in educating patients on how their medication work.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This can help to prevent long-term complications by explaining to patients the potential side-effects and how to manage them.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: However, to address the many concerns that patients may have is very time-consuming.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, pharmacists working in healthcare institutions are beset by high patient load on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They are unable to tailor individualised care for the needs of each patient and to follow-up to ensure that their concerns are addressed.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, according to the Well-being of the Singapore Elderly (WiSE) study led by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) in 2015, one in 10 persons aged 60 and above may have dementia.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This translates to almost 82,000 people in 2018, and the number is expected to exceed 100,000 in a few years' time.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of how much funding our Government pours in to subsidise drug treatments and improve access to medication, a patient's treatment cannot be optimised if he or she does not swallow a pill that is tailored to their needs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This will enable them to provide more individualised care for patients and at the same time, reduce medication-related problems and long-term healthcare cost in the community.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many seniors express the desire to age in place for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: What are the measures provided to facilitate them to achieve this aim?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It is a known fact that keeping seniors socially, physically and mentally active early on when they are mobile will assist them to have healthier and happier lives as they age.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will enable them to lead independent lives, ageing in place in their own homes and in the community for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Will MOH implement a baseline service model for all our eldercare centres to have programmes that will help achieve the above targets?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Preventive healthcare, such as preventing premature mobility difficulty or disability, will enable our seniors to live independent lives for as long as possible.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, the aim is to limit and delay the onset of disabilities in old age which more often than not are due to diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The most common causes of disability among older adults are chronic diseases, injuries, mental impairment and visual impairment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Early detection and having good control on chronic diseases can prevent disabilities such as strokes and heart diseases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Physical activities and keeping active can make our seniors stronger and lower their chances of falling, reduce their fracture rates and prevent injuries.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Regular eye checks to diagnose cataracts and other visual impairments for early treatment can also prevent disability in seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Our eldercare centres can support our seniors in this area by paying attention to their health, by checking their hypertension, monitoring their diabetes, arranging yearly eyes check and when necessary, referring them for medical help.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: As seniors live till ripe old age, frailty may inevitably set in.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: But even so, with the right measures of social and medical assistance in place to assist them with their daily living, they can still age gracefully in the comfort of their own homes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It is an excellent scheme that should be extended to other constituencies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In Singapore, we see a rapid rise in elderly population and smaller families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: On the ground, it is not uncommon to meet elderly parents who shared that they wish not to burden their children or who are struggling to get by because their children simply have too many life priorities but they are sadly not one of them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: This shift in demographics, family structure and individual attitudes has a profound impact on our society and how we organise ourselves in time to come.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: At present, we see a network of community partners offering a range of services to our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: There are also efforts to better coordinate efforts across the different partners.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is important that we reach the frail and lonely, every senior counts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How else can we better engage our seniors to avoid social isolation and better support them to age in place and with grace?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How can we leverage technology to coordinate our community networks and resources better and to engage our seniors better?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: With so much done and will be done, I wonder when and how will we know if we have succeeded in achieving our vision of ageing in place and with grace.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could MOH articulate how Singapore has progressed in terms of caring for our seniors over the past decade?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What is the state of physical and mental health of our seniors in Singapore and how has this changed over the years?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Are there indicators that MOH uses to monitor our seniors' social well-being and how engaged they are in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Chairman, Sir, the Government has been preparing for the ageing society that is already upon us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Intermediate and long-term care, or ILTC as it is known, will become a critical sector in our healthcare system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This year Singaporeans will see the introduction of CareShield Life and MediSave withdrawals for long-term care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If we add in the Home Caregiving Grant, there is another $200 in cash assistance to receive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This adds up to a potential $1,000 in cash withdrawals to support the financing of the long-term care needs of a severely disabled Singaporean.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If the affected person is from the Pioneer Generation, there is another $100 in cash assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: A Long-term Care study by Aviva in 2018 suggests that one would need around $2,300 a month on average for care, medical and everyday expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Sandwiched middle income wage earners could be facing the additional financing burden of around $1,300 a month to support an elderly parent needing long-term care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I believe this burden will become widely felt in the near future, if it is not already being felt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Already, for the Home Caregiving Grant, there is a note on the AIC website that says it will take about three months to process applications due to the high volume of applications received.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Has the Ministry done any study to ascertain the long-term care financing needs of middle-income households in the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What more can be done to support the long-term care financing needs of middle-income households who fall outside of the Government subsidy threshold?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Would opening CareShield Life to additional private insurance enhancements regulated by MOH like the Integrated Shield Plans of MediShield Life, with premiums payable by MediSave within limits be a possible answer?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Sir, in the last few years, the number of households with at least one member aged 65 years and above who hired a foreign domestic worker has been increasing.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: It seems that more families are relying on the help of a domestic worker to care for their elderly family member.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry expect a growth in this number over the next few years?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Overall, does the Ministry view foreign domestic workers as a long-term measure in supporting our aging population?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Government's overall strategy to the role of foreign domestic workers in providing eldercare?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Will this extend to the government's management of foreign domestic worker employment agencies?

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Emerging data from AWARE's research on foreign domestic workers' role in eldercare suggest that domestic workers experience the lack of training in providing eldercare as a source of work stress.

speaker: Ms Yip Pin Xiu (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Ministry consider mandating training for domestic workers who are hired to care for older persons or persons who need assistance with a certain number of Activities of Daily Living?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A lot of strain and pressure is felt by care-givers,especially those who are caring for an elder in the family while working.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These responsibilities sometimes fall on a sibling who is single and staying with a parent or both parents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They need to work at the workplace, come home to care for their elderly and make significant decisions for the person they care for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As such, what measures have we put in place to provide respite care and how effective have these measures been?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Seniors would be able to select a HDB flat with senior-friendly features and choose from a menu of care packages with optional add-on services to suit their needs and preferences.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Examples of these choices include health screening, exercise classes, personal care, housekeeping and round-the clock emergency support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I strongly believe that this will help our seniors age in place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Which service providers have been shortlisted as partners?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How much will such a unit and the care packages cost?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Will there be enough assisted living flats for all seniors especially with our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What other initiatives is the Ministry considering to support active ageing and to help our seniors age in place?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, ageing should not be regarded as a Silver Tsunami to be feared but rather as Silver Equity to be drawn upon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It is a gift to celebrate, so long as we stay healthy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With the gift of time and health, we can pursue the things we enjoy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: How would we seize the opportunities of at least 74 good years?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Since we launched the Action Plan for Successful Ageing in 2015, we have made significant strides in building a caring and inclusive home, centred on 3Cs – care, contribution, and connectedness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: From scaling up the Community Networks of Seniors nationwide, to promoting learning and volunteering opportunities, we have sought to enable seniors to age in a caring environment, pursue the activities they enjoy and contribute to others in the way they wish.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also helping our seniors stay connected by capitalising on man's best friend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: No, I do not mean a dog or cat – Member Mr Louis Ng is not here – but, you might have guessed it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As one of the 250,000 Merdeka Generation members that the Silver Generation Ambassadors have reached out to to-date, I found it really easy to access information about the various active ageing programmes via the MOL app and pick the one nearest home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This January, we launched the Healthy Longevity Catalyst Awards in partnership with the United States National Academy of Medicine, to spur bold, innovative ideas and technology to extend healthy longevity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This could include assistive devices, smart-enabled homes or job redesign solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We received more than 100 applications and I look forward to leveraging these innovations to help seniors stay active and engaged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With all our efforts, I am glad to inform Ms Tin Pei Ling that the 2019 Ageing Survey showed that Singaporeans generally had a positive outlook towards ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Across all age groups, those who were still working or volunteering were also less likely to describe themselves as old.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, 96% of Singaporeans cited health as the top concern in old age and three in four retirees wished they could have worked longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As we plan for both seniors of today and tomorrow, we must respond to changing needs and aspirations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As part of the SG Together movement, the Government will engage Singaporeans across all ages to refresh the Action Plan for Successful Ageing, so as to co-create a future where generations of seniors may thrive in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Health and employment will be key focus areas in the Action Plan, to address our seniors' top concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Of course, while we strive to make the best of our golden years, most of us will eventually come face to face with creaky knees and back pain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But if we prepare ourselves and plan ahead early, we can better cope with the uncertainty and lengthen the good years of our lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To that end, we have partnered the Centre for Seniors (CFS) to pilot bite-sized life-stage conversations, with the aim to reach out to some 5,000 mature workers, especially those in their early 50s, through collaborations with companies, union leaders and community organisations over the next two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The conversations will touch on a wide range of topics such as employment, health and family, to help mature workers prepare themselves early for the transitions in their senior years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As of December, CFS had organised some 63 lunch-time talks for over 2,000 participants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, speaking from experience, I will now like to urge all younger Singaporeans in their 20s and even younger to prepare early for their golden years, which could so easily come upon us in the blink of an eye.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Just like me – Members of this House on the right side of 50, I think would surely understand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Bone health, in particular, deserves our careful attention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: About 14% of those with hip fractures pass away within a year of fracture – a sobering statistic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Of the patients who survive, 20% require assistance with activities of daily living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Fractures can have a debilitating effect on our quality of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To reduce the risk of fracture when we age, we must start "saving up" calcium from young, before we reach maximum bone density at around 30 years old, after which, we can only maintain the density at best.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To inculcate the importance of proper nutrition and a healthy lifestyle, HPB will be conducting a pilot outreach to 10 schools on bone health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides "saving up" calcium in our youth, we must also continually upkeep and prevent depreciation of our assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In this case, depreciation refers to bone loss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: HPB will be working with Osteoporosis Society Singapore to train 300 Bone Health Ambassadors to reach out to more Singaporeans on the importance of a healthy lifestyle and diet, starting in the second half of this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These ambassadors will help to run public educational sessions, particularly in the area of fall prevention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Dr Lily Neo, Ms Tin Pei Ling and Ms Joan Pereira asked about our progress in supporting seniors to age-in-place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides expanding capacity, we are also enhancing the scope of services to better address the spectrum of care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I announced last year that we will enhance the scope of eldercare centres, to go beyond aged care to social support and preventive health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Currently, MOH funds 82 Senior Activity Centres to provide wellness programmes and social support to residents in rental flats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Services include active ageing programmes for the well, befriending services for the lonely, and information and referral for care services for our frail seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, about half of the eldercare centres will also provide higher level care services, such as day care and community rehabilitation services, to cater to those who are more frail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We also echo Ms Irene Quay’s view that community pharmacists play an important role in ensuring medication adherence in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In 2017, of some 517,000 seniors, more than 43% were prescribed five or more regular medications and seen by three or more healthcare providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Seniors who have multiple co-morbidities often struggle with making sense of many medications from many clinics and the risk of medication error then increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Thus, MOH conducted a small proof-of-concept for a pharmaceutical care service for 150 seniors at eight eldercare centres last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Community pharmacists from both private and public healthcare institutions worked with the centres’ care teams to optimise seniors' medications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Through one-to-one sessions with their pharmacists, seniors and their care-givers received tips on managing their medications, including medication packing and management of side effects, so that they may take their medications safely and independently at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will allow us to establish scalable solutions to help seniors manage their medications safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides pharmacists, community nurses pounding the ground complement the role of eldercare partners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To Ms Joan Pereira's question, we have expanded the number of community nursing posts from about 70 a year ago to about 120 community nursing posts today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These are sited at senior activity centres, community centres and religious sites, just to name a few.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We now have a pool of 245 community nurses, exceeding our target to recruit 200 community nurses by end 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As feedback has been positive, we target to expand our pool to 300 community nurses by 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Kudos to our nurses from the Regional Health Clusters, who have attended to 86,000 residents in the community, up from just 33,000 just a year ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am glad that not only do our residents cherish our community nurses but nurses, likewise, found their job meaningful, and nearly all of them have stayed on the team since the pilot started.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This year, as earlier announced by Minister Lawrence Wong, we will also be rolling out another HDB housing type – assisted living flats – to expand the housing options for seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The first one will be launched in Bukit Batok.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These new assisted living flats are meant to provide seniors with a housing option for independent living, with care available if needed, and a gotong royong spirit amongst neighbours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the past year, MOH and MND conducted 14 Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with seniors, service providers and healthcare professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, may I display a few slides, please?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The FGDs were conducted at these specially constructed mock-up flats and communal living room to help participants better imagine the assisted living experience.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It was helpful as participants could give us very specific feedback: a moveable partition between kitchen and sleeping areas, room for a full-sized fridge, and more.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We took in all the feedback and improved the design of the housing units, communal living room and basic service package.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also exploring additional care service options to support frail seniors, such as after-hours care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, what is the difference between assisted living flats and the range of senior housing options today, such as 2-room flexi-flats?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The community manager will monitor the health status of residents and link them up with relevant care services according to their needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The community manager will also curate programmes to foster a strong sense of neighbourliness, and residents can look forward to mingling at the communal space on every floor – much like the good old kampong days.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, we will set aside some units where priority will be given to seniors with care needs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More details will be shared in the coming weeks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Planning for a private Assisted Living pilot is also underway.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MND and MOH have consulted developers and care operators on this and will announce details later.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH continuously seeks to wrap care and support around Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dr Lily Neo, Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Daniel Goh and Mr Murali Pillai highlighted the importance of taking this approach for not just physical health but also mental health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I agree and we are embracing this approach.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, the HPB promotes both physical and mental health in its preventive health programmes organised in the community and at workplaces.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Like a migraine or backache, we should seek help for mental health issues early, so as to avoid problems that are more challenging to address later on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As of December 2019, we have reached out to over 300,000 persons and provided assistance to more than 23,000 persons who were at risk of developing mental health conditions or dementia.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: IMH and the National Council of Social Service (NCSS) have also been driving the “Beyond the Label” national campaign to facilitate more conversations about mental health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This way, we hope to chip away at the stigma associated with mental health and encourage those with mental health issues to seek help promptly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Anthea Ong should also be assured that physicians are bound by duty and ethics to protect patient confidentiality and to ensure data sharing and use for patient care purposes only – for all medical conditions, not just mental health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Healthcare institutions are also required by licensing conditions to safeguard confidentiality of medical records.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Specifically, our public healthcare institutions have implemented safeguards to ensure access by authorised users on a need-to-know basis.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Severe disciplinary and enforcement actions are taken against users who wilfully breach patient confidentiality.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Organisations must also comply with the Personal Data Protection Act.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, over the years, we have expanded our network of partners to ensure that persons with mental health issues can access the support they need.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, the Institute of Mental Health operates a 24-hour Mental Health Helpline.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NCSS has also recently launched a Helpbot named "Belle" to provide 24/7 access to consolidated information about helplines and mental health resources, according to what users are looking for.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Community intervention teams have also been established to support partner General Practitioners (GPs) and service providers with allied health services, such as psychotherapy and counselling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over 26,000 persons have been supported by these teams.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, persons with mental health issues who face social and family issues may approach Family Service Centres for counselling support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To date, more than half of our polyclinics provide mental health and dementia services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, over 210 GP partners have been trained to diagnose and support persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These services are available to all Singaporeans, irrespective of their specific risk factors, such as disability or gender identity.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, we agree with Ms Yip Pin Xiu and Ms Anthea Ong that care providers need to take into account specific care needs and risk factors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, for persons with hearing loss, sign language translators will provide counsellors with the necessary support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Singapore Association for the Deaf also provides counselling services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the next year or so, MOH and the Agency for Integrated Care will be engaging our stakeholders, including disability associations, to identify ways to improve mental health support.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As highlighted by Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Daniel Goh, Singaporeans can tap multi-layers of financial support, such as Government subsidies and CHAS, MediShield Life, MediSave and Medifund, for treatment of mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH reviews the amount of financial support regularly to ensure that they are adequate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, the MediSave and MediShield Life claim limits differ across inpatient treatments to reflect different bill sizes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As the bill sizes of inpatient psychiatric treatments are comparatively lower than other inpatient treatments, the MediShield Life and MediSave limits are also correspondingly lower, to cater to different treatment types.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As for MediShield Life, we have been reviewing the claim limits and more details will be announced later this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For outpatient treatment of mental health conditions under the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP), which includes depression, anxiety, including Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) – so, that is included in CDMP – bipolar disorder and schizophrenia – CHAS cardholders may tap on subsidies of up to $500 per year for treatment at CHAS GPs, and more for our Pioneer and Merdeka Generation cardholders.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Patients can also withdraw up to $500 per year from their MediSave for outpatient treatment for conditions under the CDMP.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In 2018, only about two in 10 patients who withdrew MediSave for their outpatient mental health treatment reached the yearly withdrawal limit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Further details on this will be shared by Senior Minister of State Mr Edwin Tong.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singaporeans who still require financial support after tapping these schemes can apply for MediFund from our public healthcare institutions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under this system, upon first diagnosis of their loved ones, hospitals and community partners will provide care-givers with information, such as disease progression and expected care needs and link them up with the necessary health, financial and social support services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With this, we hope that care-givers will know upfront that they are not alone, that there is an entire network of support for them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Even as we expand our suite of care services for persons with mental health, we must strengthen our multi-pronged strategy to better address mental health and this extends beyond medical care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, in the coming months, we will be undertaking a whole-of-Government review of our mental health strategy, to identify gaps and strengthen existing inter-agency efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides enhancing support for the mental well-being of seniors, we will also focus on youth mental well-being, which Senior Minister of State Lam will elaborate on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, in recent months, our healthcare workers are at the frontline, battling against the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I will also like to take this opportunity to thank all our healthcare workers who have gone above and beyond their duty to keep us safe.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are grateful, and we will do our utmost to support all of them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I share Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's pride in our nurses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It is unfortunate that some of our nurses were shunned and even berated for wearing their uniforms in public recently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our nurses wear their uniforms with pride, and I hope members of the public can appreciate and trust their professionalism and affirm their efforts The work of our healthcare workers is not any easier in "peacetime".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Healthcare workers sometimes, inadvertently, bear the brunt of patients' and their families' emotions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under the Protection from Harassment Act, the Government adopts a zero-tolerance policy against the harassment of public healthcare workers performing their official duties.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The same Act also protects them as private citizens if they are harassed when off duty.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: All our public healthcare clusters also have counselling services and hotlines for our healthcare workers if they need help.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But the best way to support our healthcare workers is not to react after harm is done but to refrain from taking out our stress on them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I urge Singaporeans to take a moment to recognise their efforts, and I am heartened by those who have rallied behind them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, our healthcare workers are truly the backbone of our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Their role will only continue to grow in importance.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As care needs increase in our ageing population, we will need a steady pipeline of dedicated healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Manpower is a perennial challenge, but on the flipside, it is also an opportunity for Singaporeans who seek a meaningful career.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have made some headway in growing the number of healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, the number of practising nurses has grown by 3.3% per annum in the past five years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In comparison, Singapore's total employment grew by 1.1% per annum over the same period.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is on top of hiring to replace attrition.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue our efforts to attract and recruit Singaporeans to build a strong local core in our workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, with shrinking birth cohorts, the labour market will become much tighter in the decade beyond 2020.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To meet our growing manpower needs, we must rethink our current approach and find creative ways to attract and retain people in the sector, particularly in the growing community care sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, we need to diversify our hiring sources.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides attracting fresh graduates, we will continue our efforts to bring mid-careerists into healthcare.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mid-careerists play a valuable role as they bring with them unique expertise and fresh perspectives from their previous careers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides healthcare staff, there are many administrative positions available in the healthcare sector too.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Take, for example, Ms Noraini, who joined Ren Ci Hospital after spending more than 20 years as a special needs educator and then as a business executive.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Noraini's experience placed her in good stead for her role as a resident care manager in Ren Ci Hospital.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nevertheless, to support her transition into the community care sector, Ren Ci Hospital placed Ms Noraini under the Senior Management Associate Scheme (SMAS).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When she completes her induction programme this year, Ms Noraini can continue to attend leadership programmes to support her development.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, we must invest in our people, especially in the community care sector, to enable the shift of care beyond hospital to community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To support the attraction and retention of manpower in this sector, MOH previously funded a total of $350 million between 2012 and 2017 to community care institutions to raise salaries for their staff.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Around 90% of MOH-funded institutions participated in this exercise.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: After these three years, MOH will factor in the higher salary levels in our funding to community care providers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We strongly encourage employers to take the opportunity to enhance salaries of nurses and support care staff and continue to improve career prospects of our care staff in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are also eager to bring non-practising nurses back to our healthcare family.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the past four years, about 500 local nurses have returned to practice annually.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Returning nurses may undergo a refresher course under the Return to Nursing scheme, and those who return to the community care sector are eligible for a retention bonus of up to $5,000.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to Mr Melvin Yong, MOH has been actively working with the union and employers on the retention and development of our healthcare workforce.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I also echo Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Christopher de Souza's call to continue supporting professional growth and development for nurses and allied health professionals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Last year, we launched the Skills Frameworks for allied health workers and medical social workers, just to name a few.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This year, I am pleased to launch the Community Nursing Competency Framework, which can be used by community nurses and employers as a guide to identify skills gaps and pursue development opportunities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From this year onwards, fresh school leavers and in-service staff may apply for the new Community Care Scholarship to take up programmes relevant for the community care sector, such as in the disciplines of Occupational Therapy and Social Work.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides training, we must also create opportunities for our healthcare workers to take on leadership positions in the sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nurses, in particular, play a leading role in care delivery in the community care sector and we must nurture those with strong clinical skills and leadership potential.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: He started as a staff nurse at Singapore General Hospital (SGH) before joining the community care sector early in his career.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over time, he took on various leadership positions and he is now Director of Nursing at St Luke's Eldercare (SLEC).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to upholding and maintaining the quality of care at SLEC, he also conducts training for the sector and collaborates with public hospitals on geriatric research.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope there will be more budding professionals who will go on to take on nursing leadership roles in the community care sector, just like Assoc Prof Poon.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, we will be introducing a new Community Care Nursing Leadership Programme this year, to groom the next generation of nursing leaders for the sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Regardless of their current place of practice, all experienced Registered Nurses who want to take on leadership roles in the community care sector are welcome to apply.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The programme will provide nurses with opportunities in clinical training, leadership development, attachments and mentorship.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Lastly, all of us must find ways to eliminate unnecessary workload and adopt best practices to work smarter.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This would include process and role redesign as pointed out by Ms Irene Quay.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope more institutions and professionals will come on board in the near future.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In response to Ms Irene Quay, employers may already choose to go beyond the minimum provisions in the Employment Act to accept medical certificates or time chits issued by allied health professionals.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In respond to Mr Faisal Manap, the regulatory scope of the new Healthcare Services Act (HCSA) includes traditional and complementary medicine services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Nonetheless, traditional and complementary medicine practitioners are already subject to relevant provisions under the Medicines Act and the Sales of Drugs Act, just to name a few.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Chairman, even as we face shrinking birth cohorts, we are also presented with the gift of longer health-adjusted life expectancy, which we can capitalise.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singaporeans are living longer and healthier and we should allow them to continue contributing, if they wish to.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is a win-win scenario for both employers and employees.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In closing, it is our unending pursuit to find ways for each of us to age healthier, happier and in a fulfilling manner.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I want to urge all Singaporeans – young and old – to help us achieve this.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: Mr Chairman, I refer to the nationwide curbing of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), an issue which I have also spoken on before on the need for us to curb AMR through legislative changes.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: AMR is a major global threat that persists and will continue to worsen if left unchecked.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: I do not speak this lightly, but the potential fatal consequences of AMR will surpass that of SARS, H1N1, Ebola, MERs-CoV and COVID-19 combined.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching
text: A quote from England Chief Medical Officer, Dr Dame Sally Davies, "The threat of antibiotic resistance is as great as that from climate change." This imminent danger is a result of antibiotic overuse, misuse and the lack of regulation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Mr Chairman, I want to start by commending MOH as well as other Ministries in their efforts in tackling COVID-19 and limiting its spread, that has impressed WHO.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Healthcare workers' calling and dedication are at the greatest committal situation presently; knowing that while looking after the sick, there is possibility that they and their family members may also get sick as a result of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope MOH will spare no effort in sharpening its future preparedness by enhancing this episode’s good practices and registering and correcting its shortfall.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There may be areas that need attention, such as being self sufficient with locally manufactured preventive and protective items, for example masks, and enhancing our health scientist sector capability to fight viruses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Adherence to a healthy lifestyle is associated with a lower risk of mortality.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It reduces the risk of chronic diseases such as type-2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Diabetes and hypertension can cause heart disease, renal failure and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Compliance on diet and medication are key factors on the outcome on war on diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Can MOH promote and motivate more healthcare providers and patients themselves to achieve it?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: A local study found that the proportion of older adults with three or more chronic diseases nearly doubled from 2009 to 2017.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: If diabetes and hypertension are detected earlier, there will be lesser morbidity and disability amongst the seniors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: All senior care centers can be tasked to assist detecting and maintaining good control for these two chronic conditions.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Breast cancer remains the most frequent cancer among women in Singapore, and approximately 6% of all women will be diagnosed with invasive disease in their lifetime.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The underlying premise for breast cancer screening is that it allows for the detection of breast cancers before they become palpable.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Small tumors are more likely to be early stage disease, having better prognosis, and are more successfully treated.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Colorectal cancer is now the commonest cancer in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The average population risk for developing colorectal cancer in Singapore is among the highest in the world.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Most colorectal cancers develop from adenomatous polyps, thus its early detection and removal reduces the risk of colorectal cancer.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Pre-malignant period of the adenoma-carcinoma sequence makes it ideal to screen for colorectal cancer and such screening has been proven to save lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Cervical cancer is the sixth most common cancer among Singapore women.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The human papillomavirus (HPV) is the causative agent of essentially all cervical cancer cases.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Because of this fact, and the fact that there are HPV vaccines that protect against infection with HPV, some countries like Holland and Australia are adopting a HPV DNA assays as primary screening methodology for cervical cancer prevention.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Will MOH adopt the same strategy for better cervical cancer prevention?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Stomach Cancer is the seventh most common cancer in men and the ninth in women here.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Every year stomach cancer takes more than 300 lives in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Pylori), a bacterium that lives in the mucous lining of the stomach, may increase the risk for stomach cancer.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: H Pylori infection is a common infection in Singapore affecting about 31% of the population, and infection increases to 71% in adults above 65 years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: H Pylori is an important pathogen that can be treated with antibiotics and should be eradicated if detected.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: A recently published report of a working group of the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) of the WHO concluded that-randomised clinical trials have found that H pylori treatment is effective in preventing gastric cancer, and models indicate that H pylori screening and treatment strategies would be cost-effective.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Will MOH raise the awareness on this finding and look into the feasibility of population based screening and prevention of stomach cancer?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, based on the reply to my Parliamentary Question (PQ) last month, after the launch of the National Adult Immunisation Schedule in 2017, the take-up rate for adult vaccination rose, but is still way below that of some other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more to promote adult vaccination?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the Government works with employers to conduct health screenings, can those same platforms, events and working relationships be used to offer on-the-spot vaccinations to workers and companies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we also do more to nudge GPs to display material in their clinics that prompts patients to ask for vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, price is always a consideration, as many would want to conserve their MediSave for other future needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MOH figures also showed that there were several hundred cases of mumps every year since 2012.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response to a PQ about measures to prevent measles outbreaks, the Minister for Health opined that passivity could explain most of the cases of children not being vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the growth of anti-vaccination beliefs worldwide should not be under-estimated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do all childcare centres require vaccinations certificates before enrollment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we do more, for example, working with pre-school centres and private enrichment programme centres to flag out cases of non-vaccinated children?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, in October last year, MOH announced new measures which would affect the marketing of high sugar drinks.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Now, I applaud this move, as consumption and availability of highly sugared drinks continue to be a great impediment on our war on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In announcing the new measures, MOH said that more details about the measures affecting highly sugared drinks would be released in 2020.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Minister if MOH has crystallised its policy on highly sugared drinks and if he can provide an update on this?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Smoking's popularity has been in decline, as more people understand the health risks associated with smoking.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I hope we can do more to discourage people from smoking and even more to encourage smokers to quit.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister provide us an update on the measures which have been put in place to assist smokers to quit and how successful has this been?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In 2018, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Health said that MOH was aiming to bring the smoking rate to below 10% by 2020 – this year.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister provide an update on how successful we have been at reducing the smoking rate?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And finally, Mr Chairman, I would like to ask the Minister about what we can do or what has been done to encourage Singaporeans to take preventive measures for the sake of their health such as getting regular health screenings done and having vaccinations performed when they are needed.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister let us know how successful MOH's "Screen for Life" programmes have been and how many Singaporeans have taken advantage of the subsidised screening under under the programme?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Are there any plans to expand "Screen for Life" to beyond what they really are, just basic level tests?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: More than 30 countries have introduced such labels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: However, with the daily sugar intake of Singaporeans more than double that of the level recommended by the World Health Organization, could we go farther?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Could MOH consider reviewing the results of these moves and if these are not effective consider adopting to some degree and in a tiered and calibrated fashion the measures that have been adopted for tobacco products, such as more graphic warning labels and packaging?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Research funded by the UK's Department of Health also suggests that removing products from choice locations within a retail outlet – for example, at the check-out counter where impulse buying is common – can reduce sales.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: While product placement is negotiated in contractual agreement between the sellers and the retailers, it may be necessary to explore nudging retailers to move in this direction in time though, of course, not without industry consultation and piloting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Industry buy-in for such moves may be facilitated by the fact that many of the firms producing high sugar food and beverage products are gradually seeking to shift revenue share to healthier products over time, as they see the writing on the wall globally.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State Dr Lam Pin Min.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Mr Chairman, for Singaporeans to continue to have good access to quality and affordable healthcare, we must press on to transform our healthcare system in the long-run, even as we face threats like COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: With Singaporeans living longer, primary care plays increasingly crucial roles in maintaining one’s health throughout their lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Our Vision, “One Singaporean, One Family Doctor”, remains relevant while we provide all Singaporeans with affordable and quality care, near their homes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since then, we have announced 10 new polyclinics, six of which will open by 2023.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In response to Mr Chong Kee Hiong's feedback for a polyclinic in Bishan, as well as Mr Sitoh Yih Pin’s suggestion to build one in Bidadari, I am glad to say that your prayers have been answered.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will be developing a polyclinic in each of these areas by 2030.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To Dr Chia Shi-Liu's query, the new polyclinics will offer similar services as existing ones, including medical treatment for acute conditions, chronic disease management, women’s and children’s health services, and radiological, laboratory and pharmacy services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia also asked about our primary care transformation journey.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This involves promoting a regular family doctor, which is important for continuity of care, especially for patients with chronic diseases who need long-term follow-up.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To work towards this goal, we shared last year that polyclinics are scaling up team-based care, where patients with chronic diseases see a regular care team.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are not far from achieving this goal in the private primary care sector too – two-thirds of Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) cardholders with chronic diseases have a regular doctor.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This demonstrates how integral private sector General Practitioners (GPs) are to our primary care transformation efforts, which brings me to Mr Chong’s and Dr Chia's queries about support for GPs in providing better and more holistic care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides supporting them in their professional development, I will share more later, we have been partnering them to anchor and provide holistic chronic disease management through the Primary Care Networks (PCNs).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Similar to polyclinics, PCNs are embracing team-based care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thanks to their support, we are on track to have at least half of CHAS GP clinics participating in the PCN by end 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She was diagnosed to have diabetes and hypertension in 2007 and started visiting Jurong polyclinic to manage her chronic conditions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2015, she switched to Frontier Family Medicine Clinic (FMC) as she wanted to have one regular doctor to help manage her medical conditions holistically.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She has also enjoyed having Frontier FMC closer to her home.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since then, she has been regularly consulting Dr Thia, whom she is now very comfortable with and who is familiar with her medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With Frontier FMC joining the PCN in 2018, Mdm Lam also benefited from team-based care, including nurse counselling, and diabetic foot and eye screening.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Now, Mdm Lam does not have to run around for multiple appointments as the PCN clinic coordinator ensures her screenings are done conveniently at the clinic on the same day as her consultation with Dr Thia.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She is grateful her care team has helped her understand her medical conditions better, and that has helped her improve and keep her medical conditions in check With the continued expansion of the PCN, more patients like Mdm Lam will benefit from this scheme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Like chronic diseases, early detection and management of cancer can make a world of difference in health outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We would like to thank Dr Lily Neo for her suggestions to improve screening and follow-up.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Oftentimes, all that is needed is a change in mindset.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Misconceptions and fears are common barriers – thinking that screening is not necessary when one feels healthy, that "it is better not to know", and that mammograms are painful, are just some of the examples.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To counter these, the Health Promotion Board (HPB) holds annual breast cancer awareness campaigns, conducts on-the-ground activities and uses social media to expand their reach.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They will continue to work with partners to encourage more women to go for screening regularly.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To enhance the take-up rate, breast cancer screening must also be made accessible and affordable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In this regard, the Singapore Cancer Society (SCS), Breast Cancer Foundation (BCF) and the National Healthcare Group Diagnostics (NHGD) introduced the Community Mammobus programme, where the first mammogram is free of charge and subsequent ones are $10 for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: About 9,300 individuals have benefited from this programme since its launch in 2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Charles Chong asked whether there are plans to expand Screen for Life to include additional tests, and Dr Lily Neo also suggested alternative screening tests for selected cancers such as colorectal cancer and also mentioned about the Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) test for stomach cancer.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH and HPB refer to the Screening Test Review Committee's (STRC) recommendations in deciding which screening tests to provide at a population level.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: These are based on robust scientific evidence to ensure that they are safe, effective, suitable and cost-effective.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: On colorectal cancer, both the Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) and the screening colonoscopy are recommended for population-level screening.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, the screening colonoscopy has risks due to its invasive nature.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Conversely, the FIT kit can be safely and conveniently administered by the individual at home.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under Screen for Life, subsidised FIT is available at all CHAS GP clinics and those who test positive are referred for subsidised diagnostic colonoscopies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Screening colonoscopies are still available at Public sector hospitals and are MediSave-claimable should one choose to go for them instead.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH and our partners will keep on striving to encourage more Singaporeans to go for early screening and follow-up, and update our strategies when new evidence arises.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mental well-being continues to be a top concern based on recent engagements with youths, which highlights the need to do more.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Dr Lily Neo, amongst many others, have recognised this and have asked how we can improve youth mental health services and make them more accessible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Indranee Rajah has announced MOE's efforts to further support student well-being through mental health education and peer support cultures in schools.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Care Corner will reach out to youths at risk and raise awareness on mental well-being and resilience.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They will also provide individualised emotional support, needs identification and peer support services, and refer those who require further intervention to appropriate health and social services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Moving forward, we will continue to take a whole-of-society approach and work with other Ministries to address youth mental health needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This includes MOE, MSF, MCCY, including their National Youth Council (NYC), on the recently announced Youth Mental Well-being Network.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As mentioned by Minister Gan, we must continue to move beyond quality to value.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: He shared that about 50% of the rise in healthcare costs is due to higher utilisation and another 15% partly due to increases in costs of drugs and medical devices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are therefore employing a suite of strategies to increase value and lower costs so that all Singaporeans can access care without experiencing financial hardship.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of these strategies is the introduction of surgeon fee benchmarks for common surgical procedures in the private sector last year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also saw a slight reduction in the average fees.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will keep monitoring the charges, seek feedback from stakeholders, and review the benchmarks with the Fee Benchmarks Advisory Committee (FBAC), so that they remain relevant and effective.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Building on this, the committee is studying expansion to surgical fees for less common procedures, doctors' inpatient consultation fees and other fee components like anaesthetist's fees, and plans to submit its recommendations later this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With these efforts, all of us will be able to make more informed decisions and benefit from greater transparency of fees.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also implemented measures to reduce drug costs, including switching to generic drugs where possible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Generic drugs or biosimilars are medicines which are clinically equivalent to branded or originator drugs and typically cost much less.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If used appropriately, both patients and our healthcare system can benefit from enormous cost savings without compromising safety and quality of care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To encourage Public healthcare institutions to use more of such drugs, MOH works with the National Pharmacy and Therapeutics (NPT) Committee every year to select a basket of drugs which can be switched, and reviews their utilisation annually.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2018, the usage of generics in the basket increased to more than 90% by volume.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to work with the committee and Public healthcare institutions to increase uptake and therefore cost savings.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have also set up the Agency for Logistics Procurement and Supply (ALPS) in July 2018 to pool together supply chain functions and resources across our three healthcare clusters to achieve greater economies of scale.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With ALPS, 85% of drugs used in clusters were purchased on national group contracts in 2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, the cost of drugs for epilepsy was reduced by up to 85%.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Building on these efforts, ALPS will work with relevant agencies to encourage greater entry of generics and new sources of drugs in Singapore and launch different approaches in strategic sourcing and procurement to keep drug prices competitive.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We must not only reduce costs, but ensure that our limited resources are spent on care that is of value.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) conducts health technology assessments (HTA) to facilitate clinically-effective and cost-effective care, and negotiates with manufacturers to attain fair prices for selected health technologies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Their work has improved access and affordability for over 50,000 patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Of note, they managed to cut down the prices of medicines such as those for Hepatitis C by more than half.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH also introduced the Value-Driven Care (VDC) programme to deliver good health outcomes in a value-conscious manner.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are extracting value for the 17 high-volume, high-cost and therefore, high-impact conditions under this programme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since May last year, we have been sharing data across providers to identify areas of improvement and facilitate sharing of best practices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As we are still at early stages, we will continue to monitor the programme's impact.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, we are expanding our scope by identifying additional conditions and increasing the period of analysis.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH and healthcare providers will work together on these on-going efforts to contain costs and ensure that all Singaporeans can access quality care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As individuals, we can also play our part too, by discussing with our healthcare providers on appropriate treatments for our conditions, and financial support available, if needed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is committed to supporting the development of healthcare professionals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Today, ACE publishes Appropriate Care Guides (ACGs) to help healthcare professionals optimise patient outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While educational visiting may be a new term to many of the Members here, it has been made available in a number of countries, including Australia, US, Canada and Norway, and is shown in many studies to improve patient care and outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through educational visiting, best available evidence and information materials on patient care are brought to healthcare professionals at their workplace, where one-to-one, focused and customised discussions are held at their convenience.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A range of clinical topics will be covered over time, the first being asthma, which affects many people of all ages, most of which are being managed in primary care settings by GPs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As there have been recent major developments in asthma treatment, it is timely for ACE CUES to bring these updates to GPs nationwide to benefit their patients, starting with those in the PCNs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked for an update on integrated personalised medicine into our healthcare eco-system.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In Singapore, healthcare demands are changing fundamentally, driven by a rapidly ageing population and increased chronic disease prevalence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is examining ways to be future-ready to ensure that healthcare delivery evolves to address these demands and adopts innovative approaches to transform healthcare while mitigating costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Work on the national strategy for precision medicine research and implementation has been on-going.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It aims to accelerate health research and develop peaks of research excellence for Singapore, and, ultimately, to improve health by identifying clinical applications that are cost-effective, sustainable and relevant.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Irene Quay asked for an update on the National Strategic Action Plan (NSAP) on antimicrobial resistance and the measures MOH is taking to optimise antibiotic use and enhance surveillance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Following the launch of the action plan in 2017, we set up the Antimicrobial Resistance Coordinating Office (AMRCO) under the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID) to oversee its implementation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To enhance surveillance, AMRCO is extending AMR surveillance and tracking of antimicrobial utilisation, already in place for public hospitals, to private hospitals and primary care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Guidelines for healthcare professionals on the management of infections and antimicrobial use are also being developed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, AMRCO, together with MOH and partner agencies such as the Singapore Food Agency (SFA), National Parks Board (NParks), NEA and PUB, is examining an integrated approach to surveillance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Singapore also enrolled in WHO's Global AMR Surveillance System (GLASS) to contribute surveillance data and learn from other countries' experiences.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: All of us have a role to play in preventing antimicrobials resistance too by using antimicrobials appropriately.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: HPB will continue its "Use Antibiotics Right" public education campaign to address common misperceptions, increase awareness and encourage patients to discuss appropriate antibiotic use with their doctors.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We generally take a collaborative approach for public health programmes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have benefited from close cooperation with the public and our stakeholders, and will continue to work together to improve public health for all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While much has already been done, our healthcare transformation journey does not end here.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As we continue to move beyond Healthcare to Health, beyond Hospital to Community and beyond Quality to Value, we need to keep in mind that success goes beyond having the right policies in place – the backing and invaluable cooperation and contributions of healthcare providers and citizens are paramount.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With that said, let’s continue to work towards achieving our shared goal of accessible, affordable and quality care for all, so that we can remain a healthy nation for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, while all of us are preoccupied with COVID-19, it is important for us not to forget about another health risk – diabetes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Diabetes can lead to health complications such as kidney failure, heart attack and stroke.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, Singaporeans face many sugary temptations in their food and beverage choices daily.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may be able to resist snacks and so on, but most people will get a couple of drinks in the course of the day which are often loaded with sugar.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include coffees, teas, soft drinks and even purportedly healthy beverages such as freshly squeezed juices and herbal drinks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Chairman, good health is not something we can buy, nor can it be taken away by people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministers for Culture, Community and Youth and Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
